'''''Erodium lebelii''''', '''sticky stork's-bill''', is an annual plant in the family [[Geraniaceae]]. It occurs on sand dunes and heaths on the Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts of western Europe. Its taxonomic status is uncertain: some authorities consider it merely a variety or subspecies of [[Erodium cicutarium|common stork's-bill]] while others consider it to be the same as the north African species ''[[Erodium aethiopicum]]''.

==Description==
Sticky stork's-bill is an annual [[Monoecy|monoecious]] herb which typically grows in rosettes pressed flat to the ground, with a deep tap root that allows it to survive through the summer on dry soils. The stem is often very short, but can be up to 15 or even 25 cm long, green or reddish in colour, and covered in dense, glandular hairs particularly towards the top. The leaves are all or mostly basal, but are arranged in opposite pairs if the stem elongates. Each leaf is deeply divided or pinnate, with deeply incised segments (cut more than halfway to the base), up to 3 cm long, and covered in white hairs. The petioles are also hairy and are somewhat shorter than the blade.
[[File:Erodium lebelii leaf.jpg|thumb|Detail of a leaf]]

There can be several inflorescences, which are umbels of 2-4 (sometimes 5) [[Floral symmetry|actinomorphic]] flowers, arising from the tops of the branched stem. The flowers are supported by densely glandular-hairy pedicels about 1 cm long. They are [[Hermaphrodite|hermaphroditic]], with 5 glandular-hairy sepals a few millimetres long and 5 white to pinkish petals 5 mm long. There are also five stamens and five carpels, which develop into fruits that look like a miniature storks bill. Each fruit is a schizocarp which breaks into 5 mericarps, each of which has a short (5 mm) basal segment containing one black seed, and a long (20 mm) beak that splits open at maturity to reveal a feathery appendage that enables the seeds to be dispersed by the wind. At the top of the basal segment there is a large, shallow pit that (unlike common stork's-bill) is not surrounded by a ridge and groove, but is partially covered by the long white hairs on the body of the mericarp.<ref name=Rose>{{cite book |last1=Rose |first1=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |date=2006 |publisher=Frederick Warne |location=London|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0}}</ref><ref name=Sell3>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 3 |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref><ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |publisher=C&M Floristics |edition=4th |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>
[[File:Erodium lebelii Fouesnant.jpg|thumb|The flowers are pale lilac and unspotted.]]

==Identification==
[[File:Erodium lebelii glandular hairs.jpg|thumb|Glandular hairs on the pedicel and sepals is a key identification feature.]]
Sticky stork's-bill is very similar in appearance to [[Erodium cicutarium|common stork's-bill]], especially the coastal variety of that species, ''E. cicutarium ssp. dunense''. The key features to look out for are the dense glandular hairs on the pedicels and sepals of ''E. lebelii'', the greyish appearance of its leaves, the pale flowers which are usually in pairs, rather than groups, and the apical pit of the mericarp, which is not surrounded by a ridge and groove. The petals must be unspotted. Confirmation can be made by a chromosome count.

[[Erodium moschatum|Musk stork's-bill]] is sometimes very glandular and sticky, but the leaflets of its pinnate leaves are almost entire, and it has large, pink flowers.<ref name="Stace" /><ref name=Guillemot>{{Cite book |last=Guillemot |first=Vincent |title=Flore du Massif armoricain et ses marges |publisher=Editions Biotope |year=2023 |isbn=978-2-36662-301-7 |location=Mèze |language=fr}}</ref><ref name=hybrids>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |last2=Preston |first2=C.D. |last3=Pearman |first3=D.A. |title=Hybrid Flora of the British Isles |date=2015 |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |location=Bristol}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The name ''Erodium lebelii'' was coined by the French botanist [[Claude Thomas Alexis Jordan]] in the ''Classe des Sciences'' publication of the [[:fr:Académie des sciences, belles-lettres et arts de Lyon|Academy of Sciences, Literature and Arts of Lyon]] 1851,<ref name=gbif>{{Cite web |title=Erodium lebelii Jord. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/6366011 |access-date=2024-05-06 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref> which is not currently available on the [https://academie-sbla-lyon.fr/allmem society's website]. Although Jordan created an enormous herbarium, the type specimens are all British material, housed at the Natural History Museum in London. Over the years there has been much confusion about which stork's-bills should be considered species, but the currently accepted account was worked out by Charlotte Henriette Andreas (1910–1989) in 1947, although she used the name ''E. glandulosum'' for ''E. lebelii''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Benoit |first=P.M. |date=1967 |title=''Erodium cicutarium'' agg. |journal=Proceedings of the Botanical Society of the British Isles |volume=6 |pages=364–366}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Andreas |first=Ch.H. |date=1947 |title=De inheemsche Erodia van Nederland |url=https://natuurtijdschriften.nl/pub/549327 |journal=Nederlandsch Kruidkundig Archief. Serie 3 |volume=54 |issue=1 |pages=138–229}}</ref>

Its chromosome number is 2n = 20.<ref name=Stace />

There are two subspecies of sticky stork's-bill: ssp. ''cicutarium'' is the common one, while ssp. ''marcuccii'' <small>(Parl.) Guitt.</small> is restricted to Corsica, Italy, Spain and Morocco.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Erodium lebelii subsp. marcuccii (Parl.) Guitt. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:881080-1 |access-date=2024-05-06 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref>

It occasionally crosses with common stork's-bill to produce the hybrid ''Erodium'' x ''anaristatum'' <small>Andreas</small>, which is a vigorous plant that has showy flowers but produces few fruits, suggesting that it is sterile. It is usually found as isolated plants in places where both parents are present. The hybrid has a chromosome number of 2n = 30 (the other parent has 40 chromosomes).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=Hybridization and the Flora of the British Isles |date=1975 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |isbn=0-12-661650-7}}</ref><ref name="hybrids" />

The name of the genus, ''Erodium'', is derived from the Ancient Greek word for a heron or egret, [[wiktionary:ερωδιός#:~:text=ἐρῳδιός (erōidiós).-,Noun,heron|ἐρῳδιός]] (erodios), because of the shape of the fruits.<ref name=Leighton>{{cite book |last1=Leighton |first1=W.A. |title=A Flora of Shropshire |date=1841 |publisher=John van Voorst |location=London}}</ref> The specific epithet was given in honour of the French explorer and botanist [[:es:Jacques Eugène Lebel|Jacques Eugène Lebel]].<ref name="Sell3" />

==Distribution and status==
Sticky stork's-bill is almost entirely restricted to western Europe, where it grows mainly on the Atlantic coast from Germany to Spain, and on the Mediterranean coast in Italy, Corsica, mainland France and Spain. It probably extends to Morocco in North Africa, but there are taxonomic uncertainties about the more southerly plants. If ''Erodium lebelii'' is really conspecific with ''E. aethiopicum'', then it also occurs along the whole Mediterranean coast of Africa.<ref name=gbif />

Its conservation status globally has not been assessed,<ref>{{Cite web |title=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/ |access-date=2024-05-13}}</ref> but in Britain and France it is listed as LC ([[Least-concern species|least concern]]),<ref>{{Cite web |title=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.xvz |access-date=2024-05-07 |website=plantatlas2020.org}}</ref><ref name=INPN>{{Cite web |title=''Erodium lebelii'' Jord. |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/96912 |access-date=11 May 2024 |website=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel}}</ref> although in [[Picardy]], towards the northern edge of its range, it is classed as VU ([[Vulnerable species|vulnerable]]). In Germany it is classed as "not threatened."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Internetredaktion |first=Redaktion: BMBF LS5 |title=Detailseite - Red List Centre Rote-Liste-Zentrum |url=https://www.rote-liste-zentrum.de/en/Detailseite.html |access-date=2024-05-16 |website=Red List Centre - Red List Centre Rote-Liste-Zentrum |language=en}}</ref>

In some counties in Britain sticky stork's-bill is considered to be an [[axiophyte]], or species typical of valuable habitats,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Axiophytes – Botanical Society of Britain & Ireland |url=https://bsbi.org/axiophytes |access-date=2024-05-13 |language=en-GB}}</ref> but in others, such as [[Ceredigion|Cardiganshire]], it is considered to be a casual that does not persist.<ref>{{cite book |last=Chater |first=A.O. |title=Flora of Cardiganshire |date=2010 |publisher=A.O. Chater |location=Aberystwyth |isbn=9-780956-575005}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
[[File:Erodium lebelii habitat.jpg|thumb|Typical habitat is in loose sand on coastal dunes.]]
The native habitat of sticky stork's-bill is on loose sand dunes by the sea. It is mesotrophic, calcifugous and xerophilic.<ref name="Guillemot" />

Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] are L = 8, F = 4, R = 7, N = 2, and S = 0, which suggests that it favours brightly lit places with low moisture, circumneutral acidity, low fertility, and low salinity.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|accessdate=29 May 2017}}</ref>

There are as yet no known associations between insects and sticky stork's-bill.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BRC - Database of Insects and their Food Plants |url=https://dbif.brc.ac.uk/ |access-date=2024-03-25 |website=dbif.brc.ac.uk}}</ref>
